ExxonMobil attributes the sharp rise primarily to **recovering fuel demand combined with reduced refining capacity, creating a tight market**:

- **Demand recovery:** Gasoline and diesel demand returned to pre-pandemic levels, although jet-fuel demand remained below historical levels because of continuing COVID-19 effects.
- **Refinery shutdowns and underinvestment:** Pandemic-driven refinery closures and a lack of investment reduced industry capacity. The broader business-environment discussion says industry rationalization took **more than 3 million barrels per day of refining capacity offline**.
- **Supply tightness and supply-chain constraints:** Investment had already been below levels needed to meet anticipated demand before COVID-19 and declined further during the pandemic as industry revenue collapsed. These capacity reductions, together with supply-chain constraints and continued demand recovery, drove refining margins steadily higher across late 2021 and the first half of 2022.

The earnings analysis additionally cites **increased demand and low inventories** as reasons industry refining conditions improved. It also mentions stronger trading and marketing margins, but those contributed to Energy Products’ earnings rather than explaining industry refining margins themselves.

*Sources: 2022 Form 10-K, MD&A, “Energy Products,” printed p. 53 (PDF p. 55); “Recent Business Environment,” printed p. 47 (PDF p. 49); and Energy Products earnings analysis, printed p. 54 (PDF p. 56).*

Walmart attributes the fiscal 2025 increases to the following factors, all compared with fiscal 2024:

| Scope | Change in operating-expense ratio | Explanations given |
|---|---:|---|
| **Consolidated Walmart** | Increased **36 basis points**, to **20.7%** of net sales from 20.4% | **Higher variable pay** because performance exceeded plan; **increased marketing**; and **higher depreciation expense**. |
| **Walmart U.S.** | Increased **44 basis points**, to **22.6%** of segment net sales from 22.2% | **Increased marketing expenses**; **higher variable pay** because performance exceeded plan; and **increased depreciation expenses**. |

- Higher performance-based variable pay resulting from exceeding planned performance;
- Increased marketing spending;
- Higher depreciation expense;
- Associate wage investments and other increased compensation-related costs at Sam’s Club U.S.; and
- Elevated technology spending at Sam’s Club U.S.

Higher variable pay is the only explanation expressly included in the consolidated discussion and in both segments whose ratios rose. **Walmart International is not part of this group**: its operating-expense ratio decreased 5 basis points, to 18.5% from 18.6%.

NVIDIA gives several related reasons:

- **Limited market evidence:** The securities are investments in privately held companies without readily determinable fair values. NVIDIA says their valuations are “inherently complex” because of the **lack of readily available market data and observable transactions**, as well as the **impact of macroeconomic factors** (Item 7A, page 45).
- **Illiquidity and inactive markets:** Note 1 states that valuation requires judgment because of the **absence of market prices and the investments’ inherent lack of liquidity**. Fair value is based on observable inputs in an inactive market (page 60).
- **Reliance on unobservable inputs:** Under the measurement alternative, the investments are carried at cost minus impairment and adjusted for observable price changes in orderly transactions for an identical or similar investment in the same issuer. Those adjustments may require unobservable inputs, including **volatility, expected time to liquidity, the risk-free rate, and security-specific rights and obligations** (Note 8, pages 66–67).
- **Judgmental impairment assessments:** NVIDIA assesses impairment quarterly using qualitative and quantitative factors, including the **investee’s operating performance and market trends** (Critical Accounting Estimates, page 38).

The filing gives these causes of quarter-to-quarter fluctuations in **net sales**:

- **Seasonal holiday demand:** Apple has historically recorded higher net sales in its fiscal first quarter than in other quarters, partly because of holiday demand.
- **New product and service introductions:** These introductions can significantly affect net sales. Their timing also affects sales to indirect distribution channels because:
  - channels are filled with new inventory following a product launch; and
  - channel inventory of an older product often declines as a newer product’s launch approaches.
- **Anticipation of a product introduction:** Net sales can be affected when consumers and distributors anticipate an upcoming introduction.
- **Dependence on a single product for a significant portion of net sales:** A decline in demand for that product could significantly affect quarterly net sales. The passage does not name the product.
- **Unexpected developments**, specifically:
  - lower-than-anticipated demand for Apple’s products or services;
  - issues with new product or service introductions;

  - failure of one of Apple’s logistics, components-supply, or manufacturing partners.

The filing attributes the charges principally to the COVID-19 pandemic’s disruption of air travel, commercial aerospace and supporting industries. Berkshire says the pandemic’s initial effects on commercial airlines and aircraft manufacturers were “particularly severe,” prompting a quantitative impairment reevaluation in the second quarter of 2020 for certain reporting units, most significantly PCC.

In that reevaluation, Berkshire considered several factors, including:

- Airlines’ announcements concerning potential future demand, employment levels and aircraft orders;
- Aircraft manufacturers’ announcements of reduced production; and
- Actions Berkshire was taking, or might take in the future, to restructure operations.

Given those circumstances, Berkshire “deemed it prudent” to **increase discount rates and reduce its previous long-term forecasts of future cash flows** for impairment-testing purposes. Note 13 adds that the charges were determined using discounted cash flow methods and reflected management’s assessment of the **risks and uncertainties associated with the aerospace industry**.

The filing also emphasizes the judgment involved: fair-value estimates depend on forecasts of revenues, expenses, cash flows, capital expenditures and appropriate discount rates. Because long-term forecasts are inherently uncertain, actual results could differ materially. Under Berkshire’s accounting policy, an indefinite-lived intangible asset’s excess carrying value over fair value is charged to earnings; for goodwill, the excess of a reporting unit’s carrying value over its estimated fair value is charged to earnings, limited to the goodwill carrying amount.

In short, the writedowns reflected a pandemic-driven deterioration in the aerospace outlook and related restructuring considerations, which led Berkshire to use lower expected cash flows and higher discount rates in valuing PCC and the other affected reporting units.

Sources: MD&A, “Other Critical Accounting Policies,” pp. K-62–K-63 (PDF pp. 64–65), and Note 13, “Goodwill and other intangible assets,” p. K-89 (PDF p. 91).

It partially offset declines in other expense categories and was one factor behind the 5% increase in Firmwide noninterest expense. (pp. 55, 62, 72, 89; Note 6, p. 228)
- **Pre-tax effect:** The filing does not present a formal net-impact subtotal; mechanically, the disclosed **$7.9 billion revenue gain less the $1.0 billion contribution expense equals $6.9 billion** before the separately discussed tax effects.
- **Tax effects:** Both the net gain and the Foundation contribution affected Corporate income tax expense through changes in the level and mix of income and expenses subject to U.S. federal, state and local taxes. ### Risk-measure and valuation effects

- **Value-at-risk:** Holding the Visa C shares **elevated average and maximum Corporate VaR, Other VaR and Total VaR**. Their receipt was a predominant driver of the **$4 million increase in average Total VaR**, from **$43 million in 2023 to $47 million in 2024**, alongside increased purchased credit protection and partly offset by fixed-income volatility rolling out of the look-back period. The second-quarter rise and subsequent decline in daily Risk Management VaR primarily reflected changes in the Visa C-share exposure. (p. 144)

  The associated reported VaR figures were:

  The 10-K does **not** quantify the Visa C shares’ standalone dollar contribution to those increases.

- **Retained B-2 position and measurement uncertainty:** At year-end, the Firm held approximately **18.6 million Visa B-2 shares** in its principal investment portfolio. They remain subject to transfer restrictions and convert into Visa A shares upon final resolution of specified Visa litigation. The conversion rate was **1.5430** at December 31, 2024, but may change. Because the timing of the restrictions’ removal and the final conversion rate were significantly uncertain—and voting rights differ—the B-2 shares were **not considered similar to Visa A shares and were held at nominal carryover basis**, rather than remeasured using Visa A’s price. (Note 2, p. 200)
- **Related legacy derivatives:** The exchange adjusted the notional shares associated with derivatives from pre-2024 Visa B-share sales. At year-end, these related to **11.6 million Visa B-2 shares**. They are recorded in **trading liabilities at fair value**, using discounted cash flows based on the estimated timing and magnitude of the litigation resolution; fair-value changes are recognized in **other income**, and payments continue while the associated B-2 shares remain restricted. No separate 2024 fair-value-change amount is disclosed. (Note 2, p. 200)

The filing does **not** attribute a specific amount of net income, EPS, capital, RWA, CET1 or leverage ratios to the Visa transactions; the specifically identified risk-measure effect is the VaR impact described above.
